pluss::timeline::today¶

Back to Timeline Factory API Reference

Signature¶

Timeline pluss::timeline::today(
    MomentClock clock = MomentClock::UTC)

Capture The Current Calendar Boundary¶

today() returns a rank-zero, one-element Timeline at the beginning of the calendar date that is current when the function is called. The result is a captured instant. It does not retain a live “today” rule and does not change at the next midnight.

This differs from now(), which captures the current clock instant without rounding to a date boundary. It is equivalent to resolving the today expression with moment(), but avoids expression text when no offset or other calendar word is needed.

Choosing The Calendar Clock¶

MomentClock::UTC is the default. It obtains the current UTC date and returns UTC midnight at its start. This is deterministic with respect to the process timezone and is usually the right boundary for globally coordinated storage, partitions, and protocols.

MomentClock::Local obtains the process-local calendar date and resolves midnight in the process-local timezone. The resulting epoch nanoseconds include the local UTC offset and any daylight-saving rule in effect at that midnight. It does not merely take the local date and attach UTC midnight.

Timeline stores an absolute instant plus an explicit display-zone label. A process-local clock does not necessarily expose a portable named-zone identifier, so the returned local-boundary Timeline retains UTC display metadata. Project it to a known named zone with tz_convert() when local wall-clock presentation is required. The stored instant already denotes the correct process-local midnight.

Example 1: Verify UTC Midnight Without Inventing Today’s Date¶

const auto day = pluss::timeline::today();
const auto tick = day.epoch_nanos().item<std::int64_t>();

std::cout << (day.dim() == 0 && day.numel() == 1 && day.tz() == "UTC") << '\n';
std::cout << (tick % (86'400LL * 1'000'000'000LL) == 0) << '\n';

Output¶

true
true

The invariant remains valid whenever the example runs; a hard-coded date would not.

Example 2: Verify Process-Local Midnight As An Instant¶

const auto local_day = pluss::timeline::today(
    pluss::timeline::MomentClock::Local);
const auto seconds = static_cast<std::time_t>(
    local_day.epoch_nanos().item<std::int64_t>() / 1'000'000'000LL);

std::tm local_fields{};
#if defined(_WIN32)
localtime_s(&local_fields, &seconds);
#else
localtime_r(&seconds, &local_fields);
#endif

std::cout << (local_fields.tm_hour == 0 &&
              local_fields.tm_min == 0 &&
              local_fields.tm_sec == 0) << '\n';

Output¶

true

Converting the stored instant through the process-local clock is the meaningful test. Requiring its UTC hour to be zero would incorrectly test UTC midnight.

Example 3: Capture Once For A Consistent Window¶

const auto anchor = pluss::timeline::today();
const auto first = anchor - pluss::duration::days(6);
const auto days = pluss::timeline::arange(
    first, anchor, pluss::duration::days(1));

std::cout << (days.numel() == 7) << '\n';
std::cout << (days.ticks().back() ==
              anchor.epoch_nanos().item<std::int64_t>()) << '\n';

Output¶

true
true

Capturing anchor once ensures every derived boundary refers to the same day, even if later work crosses midnight. Fixed 24-hour durations are appropriate for this UTC example. For named-zone calendar stepping across daylight-saving transitions, use the calendar-aware date_range() day frequency.

Operational Limits¶

The result depends on the host wall clock. Local mode additionally depends on the process timezone and host timezone rules. A clock adjustment during the call can affect which date is observed near midnight, just as it can for any wall-clock API. Use UTC when host-local policy is not part of the requirement.

See Also¶

  • now: capture the current instant.

  • moment: resolve today, adjacent days, month boundaries, or offsets.

  • date_range: advance through calendar days in a named timezone.
